entries.lesson_core_move: Compute \(p(t)=|x(t)|^2\) from a continuous-time signal \(x(t)\) and interpret it as the pointwise signal-size quantity that underlies energy and average-power calculations.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Instantaneous Power of a Signal

blocks.text: Instantaneous power is the pointwise signal-size quantity attached to a continuous-time signal $x(t)$. It tells you how large the signal is at a single time, so the rule is local in time rather than over an interval.
To compute it, take the magnitude of $x(t)$ at that same time and square it. The squaring removes sign, so a real sample like $x(t_0)=3$ gives the same power as any other value with magnitude $3$.

So if $x(t_0)=3$, the instantaneous power at that time is $9$. The same step works at every time: substitute the current signal value, square its magnitude, and keep the result as a new pointwise quantity.

That pointwise quantity is the one that will later be accumulated into energy and averaged into average power. For now, keep the rule fixed: $p(t)$ is the squared magnitude of $x(t)$ at the same time.

sections.section_title: Computing Instantaneous Power at a Single Time

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(2)=-4$, what is $p(2)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single known signal value at one time: $x(2)=-4$. Use the definition from the tutorial, $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$, and substitute the given time into the signal before doing anything else.
Now replace $x(2)$ with the given value and take its magnitude. The minus sign disappears inside the absolute value, so the quantity inside the square is $4$.
Square that magnitude to get $16$. Instantaneous power is pointwise signal size, so the final answer is positive even though the original signal value was negative.
So for $x(2)=-4$, the instantaneous power is $p(2)=16$. The same substitution pattern will work whenever a question gives one time and one signal value.

sections.section_title: Computing an Instantaneous Power Signal from a Formula

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=2t-1$, find the instantaneous power signal $p(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a formula for $x(t)$, so the goal is to turn that whole signal into a power signal using the same rule from the previous steps: $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$.
Substitute $x(t)=2t-1$ into the definition. Because $2t-1$ is real-valued, the magnitude is just the absolute value of the expression, so the power signal becomes $|2t-1|^2$.

The absolute value disappears after squaring, so the simplified power signal is $p(t)=(2t-1)^2$. The result is a full function of $t$, not just one number, because the input was a formula for the whole signal.
So the instantaneous power signal is $p(t)=(2t-1)^2$. The same substitution pattern will work for any formula you are given, as long as you keep the magnitude square around the signal first.

sections.section_title: Computing Instantaneous Power from Piecewise Signal Values

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=4$ for $0 \le t < 1$, $x(t)=-1$ for $1 \le t < 2$, and $x(t)=0$ otherwise, find the instantaneous power signal $p(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a piecewise signal, so apply the same rule on each interval: $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$. Keep the interval boundaries unchanged and only square the signal values.
On $0 \le t < 1$, the value is $4$, so $p(t)=|4|^2=16$. On $1 \le t < 2$, the value is $-1$, so $p(t)=|-1|^2=1$.
Outside the listed intervals, $x(t)=0$, so $p(t)=0$. The negative middle piece still gives positive power because the magnitude is squared.
So the instantaneous power signal is $p(t)=16$ on $0 \le t < 1$, $p(t)=1$ on $1 \le t < 2$, and $p(t)=0$ otherwise.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Zero and Larger Instantaneous Power Values

example_content.example_prompt: If $p(t_1)=0$ and $p(t_2)=9$, what can you conclude about $x(t_1)$ and the magnitude of $x(t_2)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a pair of power values, so read each one through the rule $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ rather than treating power as a signed signal.
The sign of $x(t_2)$ is not determined by power alone, but its magnitude is larger than at $t_1$ because $3>0$. Zero power means zero signal value, and larger power means larger magnitude.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert instantaneous signal power into signal energy by integrating \(|x(t)|^2\) over all time and interpreting finite or infinite totals as the signal-size basis for later energy, decaying-signal, and power classifications.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Signal Energy

blocks.text: Signal energy is the total accumulated size of a signal, not its average size. When the whole waveform matters, start by recognizing the instantaneous power built from $x(t)$.
Once you have $p(t)$, compute signal energy by integrating that power over all time to get one total number, $E$, for the signal.

This same definition classifies signals: if the integral is finite, the signal has finite energy, and if the integral is infinite, it does not. The finite-versus-infinite total is the signal-size test used later in the module.

For a constant pulse of amplitude $A$ on a finite interval from $0$ to $T$, the definition collapses to a concrete total: the energy is proportional to the pulse height squared and its duration. That is the simplest base case for the idea.

sections.section_title: Converting Instantaneous Power into an Energy Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=3$ for $0\le t<2$ and $0$ otherwise, write the total energy as an integral of $|x(t)|^2$ and simplify the integrand.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite-duration pulse: it is constant on its support and zero elsewhere. For energy, keep the nonzero interval and use the squared magnitude as the integrand.
Because the signal equals $3$ on that interval, the instantaneous power is constant and equals $|3|^2=9$. The limits stay at the nonzero interval because the signal is zero everywhere else.
That is the correct energy setup: square the magnitude, restrict the integral to the support, and leave the definite integral unevaluated for now.

sections.section_title: Evaluating a Finite Energy Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the total energy of $x(t)=2$ for $0\le t<3$ and $0$ otherwise.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite-duration constant pulse, so use the all-time energy definition $E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt$ and restrict it to the nonzero interval.
Because the amplitude is constant, the integrand is the constant power level $|2|^2=4$ on $0\le t<3$.
The total energy is $12$. This is the finished scalar value for the signal's size.

sections.section_title: Identifying Infinite Signal Energy

example_content.example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(2\pi t)$ has finite or infinite energy, and justify the answer from the energy integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a persistent periodic signal, so start from the all-time energy definition $E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt$ and check whether the integrand keeps contributing for every time.

$\cos^2(2\pi t)$ is nonnegative and repeats forever, so the signal never stops adding positive area to the energy integral. Bounded amplitude only keeps $|x(t)|$ small; it does not make the total energy finite.
So this signal has infinite energy.

sections.section_title: Comparing Signals by Total Energy

example_content.example_prompt: Compare the total energies of $x_1(t)=2$ for $0\le t<2$ and $x_2(t)=1$ for $0\le t<5$, and state which is larger.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a side-by-side comparison, so compute each signal's total energy with the same definition and compare the resulting scalars.
For $x_2(t)$, the amplitude is smaller but the signal lasts longer, so square the amplitude and integrate over its full support.
Since $E_1=8$ and $E_2=5$, $x_1(t)$ has the larger total energy. The result shows that total energy depends on both amplitude squared and duration.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the energy of a finite-duration continuous-time signal by using its support to set finite integration bounds, squaring its magnitude, and evaluating the resulting definite integral or piecewise sum.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Computing Energy of Finite-Duration Signals

blocks.text: A finite-duration signal is one that is zero outside a finite support interval, so the energy rule stays the same but the integral only matters where the signal is nonzero. The quantity to recognize is total energy, and the action to perform is to integrate the squared magnitude over the signal's support.

Because the signal is zero outside its support, the zero regions contribute nothing to the total. That is why a finite-duration signal can be handled by replacing the all-time integral with an integral over the nonzero interval only.
For the base case, take a constant pulse $x(t)=A$ on $[a,b]$ and $0$ elsewhere. On the support, $|x(t)|^2=|A|^2$, so the energy becomes a constant times the support length.

Later examples keep this same support-limited procedure and only change the shape of the signal inside the nonzero interval. The first step is always the same: find the support, square the magnitude, and integrate only over that interval.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Constant Finite-Duration Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the energy of $x(t)=2$ for $-1 \le t \le 2$, and $0$ otherwise.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a constant signal with finite support, so the energy comes from the support-limited integral of the squared magnitude. Use the same rule from the tutorial: identify the nonzero interval first, then integrate only on that interval.

Here the support is $[-1,2]$, and the constant magnitude is $|2|$. Since the signal is zero elsewhere, the integrand is $4$ across the entire support, so the only remaining job is to multiply by the interval length.
So the total energy is $12$. The new wrinkle is only the shifted support; the procedure does not change. Find the support, square the magnitude, and evaluate the definite integral over that interval.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Nonconstant Finite-Duration Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the energy of $x(t)=2t$ for $0 \le t \le 1$, and $0$ otherwise.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite-duration signal whose value changes with time, so the energy still comes from integrating $|x(t)|^2$ only over the support. The only new wrinkle is that the signal is no longer constant inside that interval, so the integrand becomes a polynomial after squaring.

Because the signal is zero outside $[0,1]$, no other time values contribute to the total. Squaring the magnitude gives $|2t|^2=4t^2$, so the remaining step is a standard definite integral on the support.

So the total energy is $\frac{4}{3}$. The support-limited procedure stays the same as before: find the nonzero interval, square the signal magnitude, and evaluate the resulting integral on that interval.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Piecewise Finite-Duration Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the energy of $x(t)=1$ for $0 \le t < 1$, $x(t)=2$ for $1 \le t \le 3$, and $0$ otherwise.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite-duration signal whose formula changes across its support, so the energy must be split at the breakpoint. Use the same rule as before: identify the active intervals, square the magnitude on each interval, and add the interval energies.
On $[0,1)$, the signal value is $1$, so $|x(t)|^2=1$. On $[1,3]$, the signal value is $2$, so $|x(t)|^2=4$. Outside those intervals, the signal is zero, so there is no energy contribution there.
So the total energy is $9$. The new wrinkle is the internal breakpoint: split the support into pieces, square each piece separately, and add the results.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Finite-Duration Signal from a Graph

image_slots.image_description: Minimal black-and-white Cartesian graph of a finite-duration signal. Draw horizontal time axis and vertical amplitude axis. The signal is zero for t < 0 and t > 2. From t = 0 to t = 1, draw a straight line rising from (0,0) to (1,2). From t = 1 to t = 2, draw a straight line falling from (1,2) to (2,0). Label the support endpoints t = 0 and t = 2, the peak point (1,2), and the key axis values 1 and 2. Keep the graph clean, uncluttered, and suitable for hand integration.

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the energy of the finite-duration signal shown in the graph: a triangular pulse that is zero outside $0 \le t \le 2$, rises linearly from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$, and falls linearly back to $(2,0)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a graph of a finite-duration signal, so first read the support and the breakpoints from the plot. Then convert each visible segment into a formula and apply the same support-limited energy rule as before.

From the graph, the support is $[0,2]$. The rising segment goes from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$, so its formula is $x(t)=2t$ on $0 \le t \le 1$. The falling segment goes from $(1,2)$ to $(2,0)$, so its formula is $x(t)=-2t+4$ on $1 \le t \le 2$.
Now square each segment and integrate on its own interval. The signal is zero outside $[0,2]$, so nothing else contributes to the total energy.

So the energy is $\frac{8}{3}$. The new wrinkle is that the graph hides the formulas, so the first job is to read support, breakpoints, and heights before applying the same piecewise integration procedure.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute total energy for decaying continuous-time signals by squaring the signal magnitude, setting the correct semi-infinite integration limits, and evaluating the resulting convergent improper integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Computing Energy of Decaying Signals

blocks.text: Energy is still defined the same way for a decaying signal: integrate $|x(t)|^2$ over all time. The point is to keep the same definition while reading the support first, because a decaying signal usually lives on a semi-infinite interval.
Use $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$ with $a>0$ as the base case. The unit step makes the signal zero for $t<0$ and leaves the exponential tail on $[0,\infty)$.

Once the support is known, square the magnitude and collapse the full-time integral to the tail on the signal's support. That is the only new move here: convert the whole-line energy integral into an improper integral over the nonzero part.
The integral converges because $a>0$ makes the exponential decay on the support. If the exponent does not decay, the same energy setup does not produce a finite result.
The same pattern will keep working when the signal starts later or is scaled by a constant: find the support, square the magnitude, and integrate the tail from the correct lower limit.

sections.section_title: Energy of a One-Sided Decaying Exponential

example_content.example_prompt: Find the total energy of $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unit step: $u(t)$ makes $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ zero for $t<0$, so the signal lives on $[0,\infty)$. Energy still uses the same definition, so start with the full-time integral and then restrict it to the support.
Now square the magnitude. Since $e^{-t}$ is real-valued, $|e^{-t}|^2=e^{-2t}$, so the energy becomes a convergent improper integral on the one-sided support.

The result is finite because the exponential tail decays on its support. This is the pattern to reuse: read the support from the step function, square the magnitude, and integrate only the nonzero part.

sections.section_title: Energy of a Scaled Decaying Exponential

example_content.example_prompt: Find the total energy of $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is still the unit step: $u(t)$ makes $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$ zero for $t<0$, so the signal lives on $[0,\infty)$. The only new wrinkle is the amplitude $3$, which changes the magnitude but not the support.
Square the amplitude before integrating. Since $|3e^{-t}|^2=9e^{-2t}$, the energy becomes the same convergent improper integral as before, multiplied by the squared amplitude.

The result is finite because the exponential tail still decays on its support. The lesson to reuse is simple: read the support from $u(t)$, square the whole magnitude, and let the amplitude factor carry through as a square.

sections.section_title: Energy of a Decaying Exponential with a Nonzero Start Time

example_content.example_prompt: Find the total energy of $x(t)=e^{-(t-3)}u(t-3)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unit step $u(t-3)$, so the signal is zero for $t<3$. That means the energy integral starts at $3$, not at $0$.
Squaring the magnitude keeps the same support and turns the integrand into $e^{-2(t-3)}$.
The shift changes only the lower limit. The decay still makes the improper integral converge, so the total energy is $\frac{1}{2}$.

sections.section_title: Checking Convergence of a Decaying-Signal Energy Integral

example_content.example_prompt: For which values of $a$ does $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$ have finite energy, and what is the energy when it converges?

explanation_blocks.text: The unit step $u(t)$ fixes the support to $t\ge 0$, so the energy test starts on $[0,\infty)$.
Now inspect the exponent in $e^{-2at}$. If $a>0$, the integrand decays and the improper integral can converge. If $a=0$, the integrand stays at $1$. If $a<0$, it grows, so the energy diverges.
So the convergence decision comes first: $x(t)$ has finite energy exactly when $a>0$, and then $E=\frac{1}{2a}$. For $a\le 0$, the energy is infinite.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute average signal power for a continuous-time signal by evaluating the symmetric long-time average of \(|x(t)|^2\) and interpreting the value as sustained signal size distinct from finite total energy.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Average Signal Power

blocks.text: Average signal power is the long-run measure of sustained signal size. For a continuous-time signal $x(t)$, we define it by averaging the squared magnitude over a symmetric window that grows without bound.

The symmetric interval $[-T,T]$ matters because the average should reflect long-time behavior on both sides of the reference time, not accumulation over a finite window. Squaring $|x(t)|$ makes the quantity nonnegative and measures size rather than sign.

In the constant-signal base case $x(t)=A$, the squared magnitude is the same at every time, so the average does not change with the window length. That makes the result easy to read: a steady nonzero signal has average power $|A|^2$.

This is why average power is different from total energy: it describes sustained size, not total accumulated area. Signals that only exist for a finite time or decay to zero will later collapse to zero average power, while steady periodic signals can keep a nonzero average power.

sections.section_title: Computing Average Power of a Constant Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the average signal power of the constant signal $x(t)=A$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is that $x(t)$ never changes with time. That means $|x(t)|^2$ is also constant, so the average-power definition should collapse to that same constant value.
Substitute the constant signal $x(t)=A$. Then $|x(t)|^2=|A|^2$, and because that quantity does not depend on $t$, it can be pulled through the integral.
The remaining integral is just the length of the interval $[-T,T]$, which is $2T$.

So the average signal power of a constant signal is the squared magnitude of the constant: $P_{\text{avg}}=|A|^2$. This is the simplest example of a sustained signal whose power stays nonzero over time.

sections.section_title: Computing Zero Average Power for a Finite-Duration Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the average signal power of the finite-duration pulse $x(t)=A$ for $|t|\le T_0$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is finite support: this pulse is nonzero only on $[-T_0,T_0]$. That means the numerator in the average-power formula stays fixed while the averaging window keeps growing.
For any $T>T_0$, the signal is zero outside $[-T_0,T_0]$, so only the finite support interval contributes to the integral.
The numerator is a fixed finite number, but the denominator grows without bound. So the long-time average is driven to zero.
This is the key contrast with a constant signal: a finite-duration pulse can have finite energy, but it has zero average power because its nonzero part gets diluted by the growing window.

sections.section_title: Computing Average Power of a Decaying Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the average signal power of the decaying signal $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$ with $a>0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the even decaying envelope. Since $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$, the squared magnitude is $|x(t)|^2=e^{-2a|t|}$, which is still symmetric about $t=0$.
Use even symmetry to fold the integral onto $[0,T]$ and double it.
Now evaluate the exponential integral exactly. The result stays bounded while the averaging window length keeps growing.
So the decaying signal has zero average power. Its squared magnitude is integrable, but the long-time average still vanishes because the fixed numerator is divided by an unbounded window.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Average Power from Total Energy

example_content.example_prompt: For the signal $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$ with $a>0$, compute its total energy and its average signal power, then state which quantity is finite.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same even decaying signal, but now the target is a comparison. Compute the total-energy integral first, then apply the long-time average to the same $|x(t)|^2$.
The energy integral converges, so the total energy is finite.

So the finite quantity is total energy, not average power. This signal has bounded total accumulation, but its long-time average power is zero because the fixed energy is spread over an unbounded window.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the power of a periodic continuous-time signal by converting the average-power limit into \(P=\frac{1}{T_0}\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T_0}|x(t)|^2\,dt\) over any fundamental period.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Power of Periodic Signals

blocks.text: For a periodic signal $x(t)$ with fundamental period $T_0$, the cue is repetition: $x(t+T_0)=x(t)$. Periodic-signal power is the average value of $|x(t)|^2$ over that repeating pattern.

Start from the average-power definition from the previous topic. For a periodic signal, the long-time average can be built from repeated copies of one full period, so the simplest picture is a signal that repeats the same level every $T_0$ seconds.
Because each period is the same, the repeated copies cancel in the average. What remains is one fundamental-period average, so power can be computed from any interval of length $T_0$.
The starting point $t_0$ does not matter as long as the interval spans exactly one fundamental period. That is the shortcut the later examples will reuse.

sections.section_title: Converting Average Power to a One-Period Integral

example_content.example_prompt: For a $T_0$-periodic signal $x(t)$, show how the average-power limit reduces to a one-period integral over $[t_0,t_0+T_0]$.

explanation_blocks.text: For a $T_0$-periodic signal $x(t)$, the cue is repetition: $x(t+T_0)=x(t)$. Start from the average-power limit from the previous section, because the goal is to replace that long-time average with a one-period average.

Now partition the long interval into whole periods. Because every block of length $T_0$ has the same squared-magnitude pattern, each block contributes the same one-period integral, so the repetition count cancels when you divide by the total interval length.
That is the one-period shortcut: once the signal is periodic, power is determined by any interval of length $T_0$. The starting point $t_0$ can be anywhere inside a fundamental-period window.

sections.section_title: Computing Power from a Given Fundamental Period

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the power of the periodic signal $x(t)=2$ for $0\le t<\tfrac{T_0}{2}$ and $0$ for $\tfrac{T_0}{2}\le t<T_0$, repeated every $T_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the one-period formula from the previous step. Because the signal is already given over one fundamental period and then repeated, compute power by integrating $|x(t)|^2$ over $[0,T_0]$ and dividing by $T_0$.

On $0\le t<\tfrac{T_0}{2}$, the signal equals $2$, so $|x(t)|^2=4$. On $\tfrac{T_0}{2}\le t<T_0$, the signal is $0$, so the squared magnitude is also $0$. Split the integral at the point where the waveform changes value.
The result is $P=2$. The only new work here is recognizing which subintervals are active and which contribute zero; the one-period power formula does the rest.

sections.section_title: Choosing Convenient Bounds Over One Period

example_content.example_prompt: A $2$-periodic signal is defined on one convenient period by $x(t)=1$ for $-1\le t<0$ and $x(t)=3$ for $0\le t<1$. Compute its power by integrating over the shifted one-period interval $[-1,1]$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that any interval of length $T_0$ works. Here the shifted choice $[-1,1]$ is convenient because it matches the piecewise definition exactly, so each constant level stays on its own subinterval.
Split at the breakpoint $t=0$. On $-1\le t<0$, $x(t)=1$, so $|x(t)|^2=1$. On $0\le t<1$, $x(t)=3$, so $|x(t)|^2=9$. The shift changes the bounds, not the power.
So the power is $P=5$. The practical rule is simple: pick any one-period interval, then choose the bounds that make the pieces easiest to integrate.

sections.section_title: Computing Power of a Piecewise Periodic Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Compute the power of the periodic signal $x(t)=1$ for $0\le t<1$, $x(t)=-2$ for $1\le t<3$, and $x(t)=0$ for $3\le t<4$, repeated every $4$ units.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same one-period formula, but now the period has three constant pieces. The job is to square each level, integrate on each subinterval, and add the contributions over the full period.
On $0\le t<1$, the signal is $1$, so the squared value is $1$. On $1\le t<3$, the signal is $-2$, so the squared value is $4$. On $3\le t<4$, the signal is $0$, so that piece contributes nothing.
So the power is $P=\tfrac{9}{4}$. The only bookkeeping is to keep each piece on its own interval, square the levels first, and then average over the full period.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify continuous-time signals as energy signals, power signals, or neither by using total energy and time-average power calculations to apply the finite-energy, finite-nonzero-power, and neither-case criteria in the Signal Size module.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Energy Signals vs. Power Signals

blocks.text: Classify a continuous-time signal by its total energy and its time-average power. Do not decide from the shape alone; decide from the two calculations.

These two quantities measure different ideas of size. $E_x$ accumulates the signal's squared magnitude over all time, while $P_x$ measures the long-run average squared magnitude. The cleanest base case is a finite-duration nonzero pulse: it has finite, nonzero energy and zero average power.

Use that rule exactly as written: finite nonzero energy gives an energy signal, finite nonzero average power gives a power signal, and anything else is neither. The worked examples in this topic will test one finite-energy case, one finite-power case, and two neither cases.

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Finite Nonzero Energy

example_content.example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a one-sided decaying transient: $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ is nonzero for $t\ge 0$ and decays as $t$ increases. Use the energy and power definitions from the introduction, and keep the notation unchanged.
That result is finite and nonzero, so the signal meets the energy-signal criterion. The remaining check is the long-run average power.
Since $0<E_x<\infty$ and $P_x=0$, this signal is an energy signal, not a power signal. The decaying transient has finite total energy even though it extends forever to the right.

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Finite Nonzero Average Power

example_content.example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a bounded periodic waveform: $x(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)$ never turns off, so the right test is average power, not finite-duration energy. Use the definitions from the introduction and keep the notation unchanged.
That value is finite and nonzero, so the signal satisfies the power-signal criterion. The remaining check is total energy.

Since $0<P_x<\infty$ and $E_x=\infty$, this signal is a power signal, not an energy signal. A non-decaying periodic waveform can therefore have finite average power even though its total energy diverges.

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Infinite Energy and Infinite Average Power

example_content.example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=t\,u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a growing causal signal: $x(t)=t\,u(t)$ is zero for $t<0$ and then increases without bound. The shape alone is not enough, so compute both $E_x$ and $P_x$.
Since the energy integral diverges, the signal cannot be an energy signal. The remaining test is the long-run average power.
Because $E_x=\infty$ and $P_x=\infty$, the signal is neither an energy signal nor a power signal. A growing signal can fail both criteria at once.

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Infinite Energy and Zero Average Power

example_content.example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a slowly decaying causal tail: $x(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}u(t)$ is nonzero for $t\ge 0$ and shrinks slowly enough that the energy test is not obvious from the shape alone. Compute both $E_x$ and $P_x$.
Since the energy integral diverges logarithmically, the signal cannot be an energy signal. The remaining test is the long-run average power.

Because $E_x=\infty$ and $P_x=0$, the signal is neither an energy signal nor a power signal. Slow decay is not enough to make the energy finite, and zero average power does not override infinite energy.
